lines.text: Aarav's uncle arranges a two-month placement at a small manufacturing unit in the city. Aarav assists the engineers.
He watches their daily work — the paperwork, the office politics, the distance between elegant mathematics and the mundane reality of the job.
Different from what I imagined. The engineers sit at computers filling forms. I fixed more things in one week at the shop than they fix in a month.
This is what Elster, drawing on Amartya Sen, calls preference change through learning. Aarav has now experienced both alternatives.
His preference for repair work is no longer based on imagination — it is based on evidence. Learning requires exposure. Without it, a preference may rest on ignorance of what was missed.
